target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is a powerful and irreplaceable hands-on learning method.
objection: Modern alternatives such as synthetic models, preserved specimens, and interactive computer simulations can meet the educational goals of learning anatomy and physiology equally well or better, so dissection is not necessary for effective biology instruction.

target: AG1’s assumption that classroom dissection is ethically and environmentally acceptable because animals are already dead or are food-industry byproducts.
objection: Dissection animals are typically obtained through inhumane and environmentally harmful means, especially wild-capture, which can reduce local populations and biodiversity; therefore the practice carries ethical and ecological costs that outweigh the classroom benefit.

target: AG1’s implication that dissection is needed for standards-based or professional training.
objection: Animal dissection is not required by AP Biology or Next Generation Science Standards, and U.S. and Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training, so the educational system does not need dissection to achieve its goals.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can replace dissection and that most specimens are wild-caught.
objection: Dissection provides tactile, spatial, and physiological realism that models and simulations cannot fully replicate, and the wild-capture framing misstates how most classroom specimens are sourced because schools commonly use already-dead commercial byproducts such as fetal pigs rather than animals taken specifically for suffering.

target: AG1’s response that byproduct sourcing and opt-out policies solve the ethical problem.
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, dissection still depends on killing animals for classroom use, and opt-out policies do not eliminate the core harm because they still preserve demand for animal specimens when effective alternatives exist.

target: AG1’s idea that dissection can be kept if students can opt out and receive an alternative assignment.
objection: Opt-out policies do not solve the coercion and exclusion problem, because they pressure students to participate in handling dead animals or else lose instructional time and full access to the curriculum.

target: AG2’s objection that dissection should be banned because it depends on killing animals and may coerce students.
objection: Those concerns call for better classroom policy, not elimination of dissection; with humane sourcing and a rigorous opt-out alternative, students can avoid participation in ways that violate their conscience while preserving dissection’s educational value.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-out and humane sourcing make dissection acceptable as an option.
objection: Opt-out does not remove the core harm because schools still purchase and prepare animal specimens, so the killing and demand remain; humane sourcing also cannot justify keeping dissection as a default when alternatives can meet the same goals.

target: AG1’s reliance on byproduct sourcing and the idea that dissection is just one educational option.
objection: The claim that classroom animals are mostly byproducts is overstated and does not negate the broader pattern that many specimens are obtained through wild-capture, which damages biodiversity and makes dissection unacceptable as a standard classroom practice.

target: AG2’s argument that opt-out still leaves underlying killing in place and that wild-capture makes the practice unethical.
objection: Opt-out is harm reduction rather than a complete solution, and in many real cases the specimens—especially fetal pigs—are already dead byproducts from the food/agricultural supply chain, so using them for education does not create new killings for the class.

target: AG1’s claim that using already-dead byproducts means dissection does not increase harm.
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, replacing dissection with alternatives does not necessarily eliminate animal materials because some substitutes may still use animal-derived parts, so banning dissection does not automatically remove all animal death or exploitation.

target: AG1’s argument that dissection is low-cost, tactile, and helps students lacking tech access.
objection: Dissection also creates environmental and health burdens such as carcass disposal, biohazard handling, and preservative or chemical use, so non-animal models and simulations are safer and reduce waste.

target: AG2’s claim that animal bodies should not be used for education and that dissection is ethically unnecessary.
objection: If animals are already produced and slaughtered for food, using their bodies for legitimate educational purposes is a better use than sending them to disposal, so dissection can be ethically preferable to waste.

target: AG1’s claim that using food-industry byproducts for dissection avoids extra harm.
objection: Turning food-system remains into classroom products can still create extra demand for those tissues and thereby incentivize more animals to be bred, raised, or processed upstream, so it does not meaningfully offset harm.

target: AG1’s insistence that opt-out plus byproduct sourcing makes dissection acceptable.
objection: The “already going to be discarded” framing cannot be reliably verified by schools or students, and even if some specimens are byproducts, supply chains are still environmentally harmful and the opt-out system leaves coercion and unequal participation in place.

target: AG1’s assertion that fetal pigs are already dead byproducts and that dissection does not create new killings.
objection: Even if the animals are already dead, using dead sentient animals as teaching tools remains ethically problematic, and school demand can still have upstream supply-chain effects that make the practice harmful.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection provides uniquely tactile and variable learning that alternatives cannot match.
objection: Unique tactile appeal is not decisive because dissection is unnecessary for the required learning outcomes and effective alternatives already exist, so students should not have to accept animal death to get hands-on biology learning.

target: AG1’s argument that dissection can be ethically justified by humane procurement, opt-out accommodations, and its educational value.
objection: Even with regulated sourcing and accommodations, requiring dissection still sends the message that curriculum goals justify killing a sentient animal, and when comparable learning can be achieved without animals, that harm is unnecessary.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-out can be made fully equitable through parallel lab time, matching rubrics, and mixed-station design.
objection: Even a well-designed opt-out structure does not solve the central ethical problem that biology classes do not need carcass dissection to meet curriculum goals, so using dead animals remains unnecessary exploitation.

target: AG2’s argument that dissection should be banned because it is not strictly necessary and parity is hard to guarantee.
objection: Not being strictly required does not make dissection ethically wrong, and schools can reasonably implement accommodation structures; if parity is difficult, the solution is to improve the lab design rather than ban dissection universally.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection can be made ethical through humane sourcing and parity while preserving unique learning benefits.
objection: The moral problem is not only sourcing but the fact that dissection uses dead animals as consumable teaching material; because non-animal methods can meet the same objectives, there is no ethical justification for requiring or even offering carcass-based teaching.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection teaches real lab science skills such as setup, measurement, observation, safety, and disposal.
objection: Those procedural and safety skills can be taught through non-animal activities such as microscopy, synthetic models, pipetting and measurement exercises, plant or yeast labs, and other hands-on protocols, so carcass dissection is not needed to build lab competence.

target: AG2’s claim that non-animal alternatives can replace dissection in practice.
objection: Alternatives may exist in theory but are often more expensive, require more maintenance and staff training, and are not implemented at the same quality in many schools, so removing dissection can reduce hands-on learning opportunities for students who would benefit from it.

target: AG1’s argument that cost and implementation barriers justify keeping dissection as the default.
objection: Budget or implementation limits do not justify using animals when dissection is not required by standards; schools should fund and design non-animal labs instead of relying on carcass-based teaching.

target: AG2’s claim that any school can simply replace dissection with alternatives if funding is a problem.
objection: A blanket ban can worsen equity by forcing schools to spend heavily on alternatives and by reducing hands-on lab time or replacing it with more passive instruction, so a phased approach that preserves dissection as one option is more realistic and equitable.
